PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM (fair-use-analysis-memo)
TO: Derek Yoon, General Counsel, Brightline Consumer Products, Inc.
RE: Project Clarity - Fair Use Analysis of Proposed Third-Party Content Uses (17 U.S.C. 107)
Basis: campaign brief v1.2, 4/28/25 email chain, Rainier article, Instagram compilation, YouTube transcript, Lakeshore report, NovaPure C&D to FitCheck, Handbook 12.4. Facts are as of April 2025; confirm current law and registration status before reliance.

1. BOTTOM LINE
Fair use is a fact-specific, case-by-case defense on which Brightline would bear the burden. As currently designed, the campaign is not clearable. Overall risk is HIGH.
- Rainier excerpts (1,100 words; Excerpt B at 480 words with no commentary): HIGH risk. Excerpt B blog use is the weakest; Excerpt A pull-quote is also weak. Excerpt C is lower risk only if actually critiqued.
- NovaPure Instagram posts: MODERATE-HIGH risk. The theme (comparative advertising/critique of NovaPure's own claims) is defensible, but full 100% reproduction, 50% of visual space, "X" marks with no substantive commentary, paid placement, and the Kimura post push against fair use. Redesign can move this to moderate-low.
- NovaPure YouTube clips: YouTube commentary version MODERATE; paid TikTok ads with no commentary HIGH (likely not fair use); Clip A and Clip C used as filler/openers are weakest.
Recommendation: do not approve as submitted; adopt the redesign in Section 6, and consider outside counsel (Whitfield & Crane / Sandra Okafor) given litigation exposure.

2. GOVERNING LAW AND FORUM
Section 107 lists four non-exclusive factors weighed together: (1) purpose and character, including commerciality; (2) nature of the work; (3) amount and substantiality; (4) market effect. Controlling Supreme Court authority: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, 510 U.S. 569 (1994); Harper & Row v. Nation Enterprises, 471 U.S. 539 (1985); Andy Warhol Found. v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508 (2023) (first factor asks whether the use has a distinct purpose or character from the original, weighed against commerciality; where purposes are the same or similar and use is commercial, factor one likely weighs against fair use absent other justification; commentary that targets the original has stronger justification than commentary using the original merely as a vehicle). Brightline sits in Austin (Fifth Circuit); NovaPure and Rainier are in San Diego (Ninth Circuit). Suit could be filed in either, so both circuits matter. Fifth Circuit comparative-advertising precedent is favorable: Triangle Publications v. Knight-Ridder, 626 F.2d 1171 (5th Cir. 1980) (reproducing TV Guide covers in comparative ads was fair use; ad format and public benefit of comparison reduced weight of commerciality; only covers, not the core content, copied; no market effect). Ninth Circuit: Sony Computer Entertainment America v. Bleem, 214 F.3d 1022 (9th Cir. 2000) (screenshots in comparative ads were fair use). These pre-date Warhol; the Supreme Court's emphasis on purpose-based, justification-focused analysis requires caution. Both cases involved limited, non-substitutive uses. Persuasive/background only: Consumers Union v. General Signal (2d Cir. 1983) (not independently re-verified here).
Remedies: Infringement exposes Brightline to actual damages and profits, statutory damages up to $30,000 per work, or up to $150,000 if willful (17 U.S.C. 504), injunction (502), and fees (505). Suit requires registration (Fourth Estate v. Wall-Street.com, 586 U.S. 296 (2019)). Section 412 bars statutory damages and fees where infringement commences before registration unless registered within three months of first publication.
Registration. Rainier: published 1/15/25, registered 2/3/25, within three months, so statutory damages and fees are available. Flag: the registration number TXu-2-412-887 carries the "TXu" prefix, which denotes an unpublished work, yet the article was published online 1/15/25. That suggests a possible publication-status error (potential 17 U.S.C. 411(b) / Unicolors v. H&M, 595 U.S. 178 (2022) issue); verify in the Copyright Office public catalog. Do not count on invalidity. NovaPure: registration status of the posts and video is unknown; its C&D to FitCheck says it runs an active registration program. Posts (3/3-4/10/25) and video (2/20/25) could still be registered within three months, or before our infringement begins (7/14/25), and NovaPure can register later and sue (statutory damages are then available only if registered in the grace window).
Aggravating facts: Tran's emails ("if NovaPure sues, the publicity alone would be worth it"; "no permission needed"), no permission sought, and the handbook's own recognition of liability create a willfulness narrative and are likely discoverable (not privileged, as authored by business personnel to an agency and then forwarded). A fair-use belief held in good faith can rebut willfulness, but reliance on the agency's "standard in the industry" view, which our handbook says is not a legal opinion, is weak.

3. RAINIER SUBSTACK ARTICLE (Content Use #1)
Work: published nonfiction first-person account; copyright notice "All rights reserved"; text invites licensing requests (tessa.rainier@...), showing an existing or intended licensing channel.
Factor 1: Weighs against. Brightline is a $187M competitor using the text to sell products (campaign objective: "competitive displacement"; CLARITY20 discount code in the blog and video). Warhol: Brightline's purpose (adding credibility, "the third-party content is what makes this campaign credible") substantially overlaps with the article's purpose, exposing NovaPure. Brightline is not criticizing Rainier's article; it is repackaging it as its own evidence, which is a supplanting rather than a transformative purpose. Excerpt A (no commentary on Instagram; one-line intro in email) and Excerpt C (verbatim voiceover, no additional commentary) add nothing. Excerpt B is the lead feature of a blog with an 80-word introduction and Lakeshore summary: the blockquote is the content. Some weight in favor: news/consumer-information value, attribution, and the lab data are Brightline's own independent contribution; but the commentary is about NovaPure, not the Rainier text. Attribution does not cure infringement.
Factor 2: Mixed to slightly against Brightline: factual/informational and published (favoring fair use), but with creative first-person narrative expression, especially Excerpt B (conversations, emotional reaction). Facts (PEG usage, meetings) are not copyrightable and Brightline can state them in its own words; only Rainier's expression is protected. Excerpt C (industry conclusions) is the most factual.
Factor 3: Weighs against. Brief says 1,100 of 4,200 words (26.2%); the supplied article file runs about 5,600 words including headings (about 20%): reconcile the count. Either way, large and qualitatively the "heart": Tran calls Excerpt B "the most compelling section ... no one else has" (Harper & Row heart-of-the-work). Excerpt B alone is 480 words, longer than needed to report the facts. Unlike the Instagram posts, nothing requires taking verbatim passages.
Factor 4: Weighs against. Rainier explicitly offers licensing; the use replaces a license fee, and the paid distribution with ~48,000-view audience overlap harms the market for first-use or syndication. Widespread copying of this kind (influencer toolkits, press kit) would multiply the harm (Campbell/Harper & Row).
Conclusion: HIGH risk. Fair use unlikely for A, B (weakest), and C as designed. Alternatives: (i) obtain a license or written permission from Rainier, with release of defamation-adjacent concerns and verification of any NovaPure confidentiality or NDA obligations (she states none, but we have not verified); (ii) paraphrase facts and attribute; (iii) quote brief passages (a sentence or two, 50 words or fewer) with real critique; (iv) rely on Lakeshore data, which is Brightline's own.
The Excerpt C text is not NovaPure-specific, so a Rainier license is also easy to justify.

4. NOVAPURE INSTAGRAM POSTS (Content Use #2)
Factor 1: Mixed. Here Brightline has a real argument: the posts are the very claims being criticized, so the use targets the original, and comparative advertising doctrine (Triangle; Bleem) recognizes that referencing a competitor's own materials for comparison is a legitimate purpose that benefits the public. Concerns: (a) the only added commentary is red X marks and rhetorical questions ("But is this really true?"), with no substantive annotation on the images; (b) the brief admits NovaPure's content "proves our point better than anything we could create," i.e., the use is a conduit for convenience rather than need; (c) channels are entirely commercial, including $640,000 paid Instagram and $520,000 display; (d) the X overlay on Post 4 duplicates NovaPure's own X icons, creating confusion; (e) the influencer toolkit would allow re-use of these images by third parties for pay (secondary liability and loss of context control). Truthfulness of the underlying message matters: Lakeshore's PEG findings support the PureGlow/RadiantSkin claims, but not "third-party tested" (Post 3), and Post 2's claims relate to Kimura's personal experience. The headline "But is this really true?" insinuates falsity beyond what the lab supports for Posts 2 and 3. Also reconcile product names: the Instagram carousel lists "Radiance Daily Moisturizer" and "PureVital Omega Complex"; the lab report and brief use "RadiantSkin," "VitalBoost" (and "VitaClean"). Do not imply the lab tested the products shown. Note the lab report is marked confidential/proprietary to Lakeshore, so consent is needed to publish excerpts.
Factor 2: Favors NovaPure modestly (creative graphic design, photos, video, though promotional and published); promotional content limits the weight. Infographic and Reel have more creativity than text claims.
Factor 3: Weighs against as designed. 100% of each post, uncropped, NovaPure's full branding and about 50% of visual space. Bleem and Triangle involved limited portions (covers/screenshots) and wholly different works. Cropping to the specific claim (the text overlay "100% Clean") plus handle would likely suffice to make the comparison. The brief proposes only a single still frame of Post 3 (one frame), though the compilation says 100% reproduction; reconcile.
Factor 4: Favorable to Brightline in part. Marketing posts have no real licensing market; harm from persuasive criticism is not cognizable (Campbell). Risk: the infographic (and Reel) could be licensed or re-used, and NovaPure's own enforcement posture (C&D to FitCheck within a month of publication of the blog post, 48-hour demand) shows it values control. Lanham Act: NovaPure's remedy for harm from the ad claims is more likely to be false advertising/trademark/dilution/disparagement (15 U.S.C. 1125(a)), not copyright. The campaign's own statement that it "creates doubt" and targets NovaPure customers amplifies that risk; the claims must be substantiated.
Separate issue (Post 2): Jade Kimura's likeness. Fair use does not resolve right of publicity or false endorsement. Use of her likeness in a competitor's ad without consent invites state right-of-publicity (Texas/California), Lanham Act false endorsement, and Instagram terms claims. Exclude Post 2 or crop out her likeness.
Conclusion: MODERATE-HIGH as designed; MODERATE-LOW if redesigned to crop, annotate substantively, display minimal size, and avoid influencer toolkit distribution and paid placement of full-size posts.

5. NOVAPURE YOUTUBE CLIPS (Content Use #3)
Work: professionally produced promotional video (drone, motion graphics, music), 215,000 views, Standard YouTube License (no CC license).
YouTube version (commentary): Factor 1 favors Brightline if Nandakumar actually critiques each clip, since the clips show the claims being rebutted (Clip B: "no synthetic chemicals"; Clip C: "100% Clean Formula," "No Synthetic Fillers"). Clip A (facility exterior, "Purity You Can Trust," music, mission statement) contains no claim to rebut and serves as an attractive opening, a classic non-transformative use; Clip C is mostly an advertisement (ends with URL and tagline). Factor 2: promotional and published; modest weight. Factor 3: 150 seconds (20.8%), with each clip taken whole, including the beauty shots and music; Clip B includes the speaker's complete statement. Take only the segments carrying the claims (a few seconds each) and drop Clip A. Factor 4: no real market for NovaPure's promotional video; low.
TikTok paid ads: HIGH risk. No commentary at all (the brief: only clip then Brightline counter-text and discount code); the clip serves as the hook for a sales message (Clip B hook, then "Switch to Brightline"). $420,000 paid spend; Clip A used as the first 15 seconds of an ad (nearly the entire ad is NovaPure footage); no criticism targeting the clip. Warhol: commercial, with a promotional purpose that overlaps with NovaPure's own purpose (selling collagen serum) and no meaningful justification. The ads use NovaPure's footage to attract attention. Also check TikTok and YouTube terms, DMCA 512 takedown risk (NovaPure can disable ads and strike the channel; account-level consequences), and music and performer rights in the audio.
Brief discrepancy: it quotes Clip C as "100% Natural Ingredients" and "Clean Formula Certified," but the transcript shows "100% Clean Formula," "No Synthetic Fillers," and "Third-Party Tested. Purity Verified." Correct before any claim is attributed to NovaPure.
Conclusion: YouTube MODERATE; TikTok HIGH.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Do not approve as designed. Under Handbook 12.4.2, written clearance is required; none should issue now. Hold production per your April 28 instruction.
2. Rainier: license or paraphrase; cut Excerpt B verbatim use; if quoting, short passages with real analysis. Confirm registration details and the TXu anomaly.
3. Instagram: crop to the claim; add substantive annotations ("Lab testing found PEG-40 HCO at 2.31% in PureGlow; label lists no PEG"); omit Post 2 (publicity); no influencer re-use; avoid full-size reproduction in paid ads; fix product-name mismatches.
4. YouTube: keep only claim-bearing seconds with critique immediately after each; drop Clip A; no TikTok ads using NovaPure footage without commentary, or replace with Brightline-created graphics quoting the claim in text.
5. Lanham Act and claim substantiation: separate review of "synthetic PEG" and "independent" lab claims (lab was commissioned by Brightline; the report says it is not a legal/regulatory finding and is confidential). "Independent" should be avoided or qualified. PEG compounds are lawful and common; avoid implying danger.
6. Evidence and privilege: preserve documents (NovaPure's C&D shows aggressive enforcement; litigation reasonably anticipated). Route communications through Legal; keep Foxglove out of legal conclusions; consider an indemnity and review of the Foxglove agreement.
7. Keep a record of the analysis; consider a pre-clearance contact with NovaPure only after counsel review.

7. LIMITS
I did not review actual images or video, only descriptions; NovaPure registrations, Foxglove agreement, platform terms, and the Kimura contract were not provided. Case citations to Triangle, Bleem, and Warhol were checked against publicly available summaries; Campbell, Harper & Row, Fourth Estate, and Unicolors are cited from background knowledge and should be cite-checked.
